content.heading: How to Start a Pollinator Watch
content.text: Pick a single flowering plant — a blooming willow, a patch of dandelions, a blueberry bush — and spend 15 minutes just watching. Note what visits: how big is it, what color, does it hover or land, does it crawl into the flower or just touch the surface? You'll quickly start seeing patterns. Bumblebees land heavily and push into flowers. Butterflies perch on petals with wings folded or spread. Hoverflies hover and dart. Mining bees move methodically from flower to flower, packing pollen onto their hind legs. The app iNaturalist is excellent for documenting what you see — photograph the visitor on the flower, upload it, and the community will help identify it. Over time, you build a personal record of what pollinators are active where and when. For a more systematic survey of what's in your area, try bee bowls — place shallow dishes or bowls (yellow, blue, and white work best) filled with soapy water in a sunny spot near flowers. Bees are attracted to the colors and the soapy water prevents them from flying away. It's the same method researchers use to inventory bee diversity at field sites, and it can reveal species you'd never spot by eye. For citizen science, consider joining the Great Sunflower Project, Bumble Bee Watch, or the Xerces Society's community science programs. Your backyard observations contribute to real conservation research.

content.heading: A Spring Pollinator Calendar
content.text: Late February to March — mourning cloaks emerge on warm days; skunk cabbage attracts early flies. Late March to mid-April — first mining bees (Andrena) on willows and red maple; cellophane bees (Colletes) in sandy areas; commas and question marks basking on paths. Mid-April to early May — bumblebee queens foraging heavily on cherry blossoms and dead nettle; spring azures fluttering in the understory; mason bees nesting in cavities; carpenter bees hovering around wood structures. May — the full orchestra arrives: swallowtails on lilacs, hummingbird clearwings on honeysuckle, leafcutter bees cutting circles from rose leaves, metallic green sweat bees on everything, ruby-throated hummingbirds on wild columbine. Late May to June — monarch butterflies arrive from the south; painted ladies on clover and asters; bumblebee colonies growing rapidly with worker bees emerging; blueberry buzz pollination in full swing.

Five pollinators to learn first this spring: (1) Bumblebee queen — big, fuzzy, flying low and slow in April, desperately feeding. (2) Mourning cloak butterfly — dark maroon with yellow border, first butterfly of spring, found basking on paths. (3) Mining bee (Andrena) — small, fuzzy, visiting willows and dandelions, nesting in bare ground. (4) Hoverfly — yellow-and-black striped, hovers motionless, harmless bee mimic. (5) Carpenter bee — large, shiny black, hovering around porches and decks. Learn these five and you've met the major pollinator guilds.

title: Vernal Pools: The Invisible Ecosystems
subtitle: Temporary spring ponds that sustain some of New England's most fascinating wildlife

content.text: They appear in late winter, fill with snowmelt and rain, teem with life for a few months, and then dry up completely by midsummer. Vernal pools are among the most important and least understood habitats in New England — temporary wetlands that exist for only part of the year but support species found nowhere else. If you've walked past a muddy depression in the woods in April and thought it was just a puddle, you may have been standing at the edge of an ecosystem millions of years old.

content.heading: What Makes a Vernal Pool
content.text: A vernal pool is a seasonal body of water that fills in spring (the name comes from the Latin "vernalis," meaning "of spring"), holds water long enough for certain animals to complete their breeding cycle, and dries out by late summer or fall. The drying is the critical feature — it's what makes vernal pools special. Because they dry up, vernal pools cannot support permanent fish populations. And because they have no fish, they become safe havens for amphibians and invertebrates that would be devoured in any pond with a resident bass or sunfish. This fish-free window is the entire evolutionary reason these animals use vernal pools. They've traded the risk of drought for the guarantee of no predatory fish. Vernal pools form in depressions in the forest floor — old root holes, glacial kettles, rocky basins, and clay-bottomed low spots where water collects. They range from a few feet across to several acres. Most are small, inconspicuous, and easy to walk past without noticing.

content.heading: The Big Night: Salamander Migration
content.text: The most dramatic event in the vernal pool calendar is the mass migration of spotted salamanders (Ambystoma maculatum) on the first warm, rainy nights of early spring. When conditions align — temperatures above 40°F, steady rain, ideally after dark — hundreds or even thousands of spotted salamanders emerge simultaneously from their underground burrows and walk to the nearest vernal pool to breed. This is called "Big Night" among naturalists, and it's one of New England's great wildlife spectacles. Spotted salamanders are stunning animals — 6 to 9 inches long, jet black with two rows of bright yellow spots. They spend most of their lives underground, invisible, and many people who live near thriving populations have no idea they exist. But on Big Night, they're suddenly everywhere — crossing roads, climbing over leaf litter, converging on pools from all directions. The migration can happen anytime from late February (southern Connecticut) to late April (northern Maine), and the exact night is unpredictable until conditions come together. Blue-spotted salamanders (Ambystoma laterale) and Jefferson salamanders (Ambystoma jeffersonianum) migrate on the same nights but are less conspicuous — slimmer, darker, and less abundant. Marbled salamanders (Ambystoma opacum) are the oddball — they breed in the fall, laying eggs in dry pool basins that hatch when autumn rains fill the pool.

content.heading: Wood Frogs: The Loudest Inhabitants
content.text: If spotted salamanders are the silent stars of vernal pools, wood frogs (Lithobates sylvaticus) are the noisy ones. Wood frogs arrive at pools around the same time as the salamanders — sometimes the same night — and immediately begin a deafening chorus. Their call sounds like quacking ducks or a room full of people laughing. A pool with dozens of calling wood frogs can be heard from hundreds of feet away. Wood frogs are remarkable for another reason: they survive winter by literally freezing. Up to 65% of a wood frog's body water turns to ice during winter hibernation. Their heart stops. Their brain shows no activity. Special proteins and high concentrations of glucose act as cryoprotectants, preventing fatal ice crystal damage to cells. When temperatures rise in spring, they thaw, their heart restarts, and within hours they're hopping toward the nearest pool to breed. The breeding frenzy is intense and brief — usually just a few days. Females lay globular egg masses attached to submerged branches, often communally, creating clusters of dozens of masses. Then the adults leave and don't return until the following spring. The tadpoles must develop legs, absorb their tails, and leave the pool before it dries — a race against evaporation.

content.alt: Wood frog (Lithobates sylvaticus) — dark mask across eyes, tan body
content.caption: Wood frog — survives winter by literally freezing solid, then thaws and hops to the nearest pool to breed

content.heading: Spring Peepers and the Chorus
content.text: Spring peepers (Pseudacris crucifer) are not strictly vernal pool specialists — they'll breed in any shallow, fishless wetland — but they're so intertwined with the spring pool experience that no vernal pool article would be complete without them. Their high-pitched "peep-peep-peep" is the quintessential sound of spring in New England, audible on warm evenings from March onward. Each peeper is tiny — barely an inch long — with a distinctive dark X on its back (the species name "crucifer" means cross-bearer). Males call from emergent vegetation at the water's edge, inflating a vocal sac nearly as large as their body. A full chorus of peepers can exceed 90 decibels — louder than a lawnmower. Gray treefrogs (Dryophytes versicolor) and American toads (Anaxyrus americanus) join the chorus later in spring. The toad's long, musical trill — sustained for 10 to 30 seconds at a stretch — is one of the loveliest sounds in nature and carries far across the landscape on warm May evenings.

content.alt: Spring peeper (Pseudacris crucifer) — tiny frog with dark X on its back, inflating vocal sac
content.caption: Spring peeper — barely an inch long, with the dark X on its back that gives it the name 'crucifer' (cross-bearer)

content.heading: Fairy Shrimp: Ancient Crustaceans in Temporary Ponds
content.text: Perhaps the most surprising vernal pool inhabitants are fairy shrimp (Eubranchipus) — translucent, inch-long crustaceans that swim upside down through the water column, filtering algae and detritus. They look otherworldly, like tiny, delicate ghosts with feathery legs rippling in waves. Fairy shrimp are obligate vernal pool species — they cannot survive in permanent water because fish eat them instantly. Their life cycle is entirely tied to the temporary pool. Adults appear in late winter or early spring, grow rapidly, mate, and produce drought-resistant eggs (called cysts) that sink to the pool bottom. When the pool dries, the adults die, but the cysts survive — buried in dry leaf litter and mud through summer, fall, and winter, sometimes for years. When water returns the following spring, the cysts hatch and the cycle begins again. New England has several fairy shrimp species, including Eubranchipus vernalis (the vernal fairy shrimp) and E. bundyi. Finding fairy shrimp in a pool is a strong indicator that you've found a legitimate, functioning vernal pool — they are one of the official "indicator species" used in vernal pool certification.

content.heading: The Food Web in a Puddle
content.text: A vernal pool may look like a simple puddle, but it contains a surprisingly complex food web. Decomposing leaves that fell into the dry basin in autumn form the base — bacteria and fungi colonize them, and invertebrates shred and consume the decaying material. Zooplankton, fairy shrimp, and aquatic insects graze on algae and microorganisms. Predaceous diving beetles (Dytiscus) are the top invertebrate predators — aggressive, fast-swimming beetles that attack tadpoles, fairy shrimp, and even small salamander larvae. Both the adult beetles and their larvae (called "water tigers") are formidable hunters. Caddisfly larvae build portable cases from bits of leaf, twig, and sand grains, crawling across the pool bottom like tiny armored vehicles. Dragonfly and damselfly nymphs — which can spend months developing underwater — are ambush predators that snatch passing prey with an extendable jaw called a labium that shoots forward in milliseconds. Spotted salamander larvae are near the top of the pool food chain. They start as tiny, gilled creatures feeding on zooplankton, then grow large enough to consume fairy shrimp, insect larvae, and even smaller salamander larvae. The entire food web must complete its work before the pool dries — a ticking clock that drives intense competition.

content.heading: The Upland Connection
content.text: Here's something most people don't realize: vernal pool animals don't actually live in vernal pools. They visit pools briefly to breed, but they spend the vast majority of their lives — 10 to 11 months of the year — in the surrounding upland forest. Spotted salamanders live in small mammal burrows, under logs, and in rock crevices, sometimes hundreds of meters from the nearest pool. Wood frogs overwinter under leaf litter on the forest floor. This means that protecting a vernal pool without protecting the surrounding forest is meaningless. Research suggests that a buffer of at least 100 to 200 meters of intact forest around a pool is necessary to sustain the breeding populations that depend on it. Clear-cutting, development, or road construction within this zone can eliminate pool populations even if the pool itself is untouched. Roads are a particularly lethal threat. When salamanders and frogs migrate to and from pools on rainy spring nights, they must cross any roads in their path. A single road between a population's upland habitat and its breeding pool can cause annual mortality rates of 50 to 90 percent — enough to collapse a population within a few years.

content.heading: Newts: The Year-Round Residents
content.text: Eastern newts (Notophthalmus viridescens) have the most complex life cycle of any New England amphibian, and they bridge the gap between vernal pools and permanent wetlands. They start as aquatic larvae in pools and ponds. Then they transform into a terrestrial juvenile stage called a red eft — bright orange-red with vivid red spots, a walking advertisement of the toxins in their skin. Red efts wander the forest floor for 2 to 7 years, and they're what most people encounter — crossing trails after rain, tucked under logs, sometimes in surprisingly dry locations far from water. Eventually, the eft transforms again into an olive-green aquatic adult and returns to water permanently, developing a flattened tail for swimming. Adults can live in permanent ponds (unlike the obligate vernal pool species), but they also use deeper vernal pools. Their skin toxins — tetrodotoxin, the same compound found in pufferfish — make them unpalatable to fish, so they can survive in waters where spotted salamanders and wood frogs cannot.

content.alt: Eastern newt (Notophthalmus viridescens) — bright orange-red eft stage with red spots
content.caption: Eastern newt in its bright red eft stage — a walking warning sign of the tetrodotoxin in its skin

content.heading: Turtles and the Pool Margin
content.text: Several New England turtle species are associated with vernal pools, though they use them differently than amphibians. Spotted turtles (Clemmys guttata) — small, dark-shelled turtles with bright yellow polka dots — are among the earliest turtles to emerge from hibernation and are frequently found in and around vernal pools in March and April, feeding on amphibian eggs and invertebrates. They're a species of conservation concern throughout New England due to habitat loss and collection for the pet trade. Wood turtles (Glyptemys insculpta) are semi-terrestrial turtles that wander through forests and along streams, sometimes visiting vernal pools to feed. Their sculpted, pyramid-patterned shells are beautiful and distinctive. They're remarkably intelligent for reptiles — studies have shown they can navigate mazes as well as rats. Snapping turtles (Chelydra serpentina) occasionally visit larger vernal pools, and painted turtles (Chrysemys picta) may use pools that connect to broader wetland systems. But these are visitors and opportunists, not vernal pool specialists.

content.heading: How to Find Vernal Pools
content.text: The best time to find vernal pools is early spring — March through April — when they're full and active. Walk through deciduous forest on low ground, in valleys, and along the bases of slopes. Listen for wood frog chorus (quacking) and peepers (high-pitched peeping) on warm evenings, especially after rain. A headlamp on a warm, rainy night in early April is the ultimate vernal pool discovery tool — you'll find the pools by sound, and once you're there, you'll see salamanders, frogs, and invertebrates in the beam. During the day, look for egg masses. Spotted salamander egg masses are softball-sized gelatinous globs, clear or milky white, attached to submerged branches. Wood frog egg masses are similar but communal — often dozens of grape-sized masses clustered together near the surface. If you find egg masses, you've confirmed a functioning vernal pool. Other clues: dark, tea-colored water stained by tannins from decomposing leaves. Watermarks on tree trunks showing seasonal high water lines. Patches of sphagnum moss around the margins. Sedges (Carex) and skunk cabbage in the wet zone. And in summer, a conspicuous depression with flat, dark, compressed leaves and no understory vegetation — the ghost of where water stood.

content.heading: Threats and Protection
content.text: Vernal pools are among the most threatened habitats in New England. Because they're small, temporary, and often don't look like "real" wetlands, they've historically been treated as insignificant — filled, drained, graded, or paved over by the thousands. Massachusetts is the only New England state with explicit vernal pool protection laws, and even there, pools must be formally certified to receive legal protection. The certification process requires documenting obligate indicator species — spotted salamanders, wood frogs, or fairy shrimp — by finding their egg masses or larvae. Climate change poses a newer threat. Warmer springs can cause pools to dry earlier, before larvae have completed development. A pool that historically held water into July might now dry by late May — not enough time for spotted salamander larvae, which need 2 to 4 months of water. Conversely, some pools may hold water long enough to be colonized by fish, eliminating their value as fishless refugia. If you find a vernal pool on your property or in your community, consider getting it certified. In Massachusetts, the Natural Heritage & Endangered Species Program accepts vernal pool certifications from citizens. Even outside Massachusetts, documenting pools through state natural heritage programs contributes to conservation planning.

content.heading: A Visit Through the Seasons
content.text: A single vernal pool, visited monthly, reveals a complete story arc. In February, it's a frozen or nearly frozen depression under snow. In March, snowmelt fills it and the first salamanders arrive on rainy nights. In April, wood frogs are chorusing, egg masses dot the water, fairy shrimp are swimming, and the pool is at peak water level. In May, tadpoles and salamander larvae are growing, dragonfly nymphs are hunting, and diving beetles patrol the depths. In June, the first metamorphosed froglets emerge with tiny stubs of tails still absorbing. By July, the pool is shrinking — a race between drying mud and developing larvae. In August, it's often just a damp depression with compressed leaves. In September and October, fallen leaves accumulate in the dry basin, providing next year's food base. And in November, marbled salamanders lay their eggs in the empty pool, trusting that water will return. The cycle is ancient, reliable, and endlessly fascinating — and it all happens in what most people would dismiss as a woodland puddle.

Want to witness Big Night? Watch the weather starting in late March. When you get a rainy evening with temperatures above 40°F after a stretch of cold weather, head to a known vernal pool area after dark with a headlamp and rain gear. Move slowly, watch the ground — spotted salamanders will be walking deliberately toward water. Drive slowly on rural roads near wetlands, as thousands of amphibians may be crossing. Some communities organize volunteer road-crossing patrols to carry salamanders safely across busy roads. Check with your local land trust or conservation commission to see if one operates near you.

title: Invasive Species of New England: A Field Guide
subtitle: Know your enemy — the plants, insects, and other invaders reshaping New England's ecosystems

content.text: Walk into almost any forest, field, or wetland in New England and you'll find invasive species. They choke forest understories, smother stream banks, displace native wildflowers, and alter ecosystems in ways that cascade through entire food webs. But here's the thing — many people walk past them every day without recognizing them. Learning to identify the most damaging invaders is the first step toward doing something about them. Whether you're signing up for a volunteer removal day or just want to know what you're looking at, this guide covers the invasive species you're most likely to encounter and how to tell them from native lookalikes.

content.heading: What Makes a Species Invasive
content.text: Not every non-native species is invasive. Plenty of introduced plants coexist harmlessly with native ecosystems — daylilies along roadsides, for instance. An invasive species is one that spreads aggressively beyond where it was planted, displaces native species, and causes measurable ecological or economic harm. Most invasive plants share a set of traits: they grow fast, reproduce prolifically (often through both seeds and vegetative spreading), tolerate a wide range of conditions, and — crucially — they've left behind the insects, diseases, and herbivores that kept them in check in their native range. A Japanese barberry bush in Japan is eaten by dozens of insect species. The same bush in Massachusetts has almost no natural enemies, so it grows unchecked.

content.heading: The Big Five: Plants You'll Pull the Most
content.text: If you volunteer for invasive plant removal in New England, you'll spend most of your time on these five species. They're the most widespread, the most damaging, and the ones conservation groups target most aggressively. Garlic mustard (Alliaria petiolata) is a biennial herb that invades rich deciduous forests — exactly the same habitat as spring ephemerals. First-year plants form a low rosette of kidney-shaped, scalloped leaves. Second-year plants bolt to 2–3 feet tall with small white four-petaled flowers and long, narrow seed pods. The entire plant smells like garlic when crushed. Its real damage is underground: garlic mustard releases chemicals that disrupt the mycorrhizal fungi that native plants depend on, effectively poisoning the soil for its competitors. Japanese barberry (Berberis thunbergii) forms dense, thorny thickets in forest understories, shading out native wildflowers and creating humid microclimates that increase tick populations — studies have shown significantly higher tick densities in barberry-infested areas. Small, oval leaves, arching thorny branches, and bright red berries that persist through winter. Originally planted as an ornamental hedge, it's now one of the worst invaders in the region. Multiflora rose (Rosa multiflora) was deliberately planted by the millions in the mid-20th century for erosion control and highway barriers — one of the great ecological mistakes of the era. It forms impenetrable, arching, thorny thickets up to 15 feet tall. White flowers in spring, clusters of small red rose hips in fall. You'll know it by the fringed stipules at the base of each leaf stalk — a key feature that separates it from native roses.

content.heading: The Big Five, Continued
content.text: Oriental bittersweet (Celastrus orbiculatus) is a woody vine that climbs trees, eventually strangling and toppling them under its weight. It's immediately recognizable in autumn and winter by its clusters of bright yellow-orange capsules splitting open to reveal red berries — decorative, which is exactly why people spread it. Don't confuse it with native American bittersweet (Celastrus scandens), which has berry clusters only at the tips of stems, not along the entire length. Oriental bittersweet has berries distributed along the vine at every leaf node. Bush honeysuckles (Lonicera morrowii, L. tatarica, L. maackii) are among the earliest shrubs to leaf out in spring and the last to drop leaves in fall, giving them a competitive advantage over native species that play by the normal schedule. They produce abundant red or orange berries that birds eat and spread everywhere. The telltale feature: snap a honeysuckle stem in half. If the pith (center) is hollow, it's an invasive Asian honeysuckle. Native honeysuckles (like Lonicera canadensis) have solid pith.

content.heading: Forest Understory Invaders
content.text: Beyond the Big Five, several other species dominate New England's invaded forests. Burning bush (Euonymus alatus) is planted everywhere for its brilliant red fall color, but it escapes readily into forests. The stems have distinctive corky "wings" — ridged flanges running along the bark — that make it identifiable even in winter. Common buckthorn (Rhamnus cathartica) and glossy buckthorn (Frangula alnus) are shrubs or small trees that form dense stands, holding their green leaves well into November — long after native species have dropped theirs. That's actually a quick way to spot them in fall: any shrub still green in a leafless November forest is likely buckthorn. Buckthorn berries are mildly toxic to birds, causing diarrhea that spreads seeds rapidly but provides poor nutrition compared to native berries. Norway maple (Acer platanoides) looks similar to sugar maple but is far more shade-tolerant, allowing it to establish dense stands that crowd out native trees. The key ID feature: break a Norway maple leaf stalk and it oozes milky white sap. Sugar maple sap is clear. Norway maple leaves also tend to be wider, darker green, and the leaf lobes have fewer teeth. Autumn olive (Elaeagnus umbellata) is a shrub or small tree with distinctive silvery-scaled undersides on its leaves. It produces enormous quantities of small red berries and fixes nitrogen in the soil — which sounds beneficial but actually alters soil chemistry in ways that favor other invasive species over natives.

content.heading: The Streamside and Wetland Invaders
content.text: Some of New England's most aggressive invaders specialize in wet areas. Japanese knotweed (Reynoutria japonica) is often called the most destructive invasive plant in the region. It forms dense, bamboo-like stands 6 to 10 feet tall along stream banks, roads, and disturbed areas. Hollow, jointed green stems with reddish speckles; large, shield-shaped leaves; sprays of tiny white flowers in late summer. It spreads almost entirely through rhizomes — underground stems that can extend 20 feet from the parent plant and penetrate asphalt and concrete. A fragment of rhizome as small as half an inch can regenerate an entire plant. Cutting it stimulates growth. Mowing it spreads fragments. It is extraordinarily difficult to eradicate. Purple loosestrife (Lythrum salicaria) turns wetlands into stunning magenta displays in July and August — and that beauty is the problem. A single plant can produce 2 to 3 million seeds per year, and dense stands crowd out native cattails, sedges, and other wetland plants that wildlife depends on. Biological control using European beetles (Galerucella species) that feed specifically on loosestrife has been one of the most successful invasive species management programs in North America. Phragmites (Phragmites australis) — common reed — forms towering, dense monocultures in marshes, ditches, and coastal wetlands, reaching 12 to 15 feet tall. Native Phragmites exists in New England but is rare and grows in small, sparse patches. The invasive form grows in massive, impenetrable stands. If you see a wall of tall reeds along a highway or marsh edge, it's almost certainly the invasive type.

content.heading: The Dangerous Ones: Plants That Can Hurt You
content.text: Two invasive plants in New England are genuine health hazards. Giant hogweed (Heracleum mantegazzianum) is the most dangerous plant in the region. It looks like a massive version of Queen Anne's lace — 10 to 15 feet tall with huge umbrella-shaped flower heads and thick, purple-spotted stems. Its sap contains furanocoumarins that cause severe phytophotodermatitis: when sap contacts skin and is then exposed to sunlight, it causes painful blisters and burns that can leave permanent scars. If you find giant hogweed, do not touch it. Report it to your state's department of agriculture. Wild parsnip (Pastinaca sativa) — while not in the same league as hogweed — causes similar but milder photosensitive skin reactions. It's a yellow-flowered member of the carrot family that's common along roadsides throughout New England. Wear long sleeves and gloves when working near either species.

content.heading: Vines That Smother
content.text: Invasive vines are particularly destructive because they climb into the canopy, blocking light from the trees that support them and eventually killing them. Beyond oriental bittersweet (covered above), watch for: Japanese honeysuckle (Lonicera japonica) — an evergreen to semi-evergreen vine that blankets shrubs and small trees. Fragrant white-to-yellow flowers, but it forms dense mats that smother everything underneath. Black swallowwort (Vincetoxicum nigrum) and pale swallowwort (V. rossicum) are less well-known but rapidly spreading. They're twining vines in the milkweed family that produce pods resembling milkweed, which is a problem — monarch butterflies sometimes lay eggs on swallowwort, but the larvae can't survive on it. It's an ecological trap. Mile-a-minute vine (Persicaria perfoliata) is a newer arrival — a barbed, triangular-leaved vine that can grow 6 inches per day, smothering everything in its path. It's still relatively uncommon in most of New England but spreading northward.

content.heading: Invasive Insects: The Invisible Destruction
content.text: Some of the most devastating invasives in New England aren't plants at all. Emerald ash borer (Agrilus planipennis) — a metallic green beetle from Asia — has killed hundreds of millions of ash trees across North America since its discovery in Michigan in 2002. It's now present throughout New England. The larvae bore through the inner bark, cutting off the tree's nutrient transport, and infested trees die within 2 to 5 years. White ash, green ash, and black ash are all vulnerable. Entire forests are losing their ash component, with cascading effects on the species that depend on them. Hemlock woolly adelgid (Adelges tsugae) — a tiny, aphid-like insect — is killing eastern hemlocks throughout southern New England. It appears as white, woolly masses at the base of hemlock needles. Infested trees lose their needles and typically die within 4 to 10 years. Since hemlock creates unique cool, shady habitats along streams, its loss transforms entire stream ecosystems. Spongy moth (Lymantria dispar, formerly called gypsy moth) periodically defoliates millions of acres of oak and other hardwood forests. During outbreak years, caterpillars can strip trees bare. Most healthy trees can survive one or two years of defoliation, but repeated attacks weaken them and make them vulnerable to other stresses. Japanese beetles (Popillia japonica) are the iridescent green-and-copper beetles that skeletonize rose bushes, grapes, and dozens of other plants in midsummer. Their larvae (white grubs) feed on grass roots, causing brown patches in lawns.

content.alt: Spongy moth (Lymantria dispar) — caterpillar that defoliates millions of acres of oak forest
content.caption: Spongy moth caterpillar — during outbreak years, these can strip entire forests bare

content.heading: Native Lookalikes: Don't Pull the Wrong Plant
content.text: One of the biggest risks during invasive removal is accidentally pulling native plants that resemble invasives. Here are the key distinctions to learn. American bittersweet (Celastrus scandens) vs. oriental bittersweet (C. orbiculatus): native has berry clusters only at branch tips; invasive has berries at every leaf node along the vine. Pull the wrong one and you're removing a declining native species. Native honeysuckle (Lonicera canadensis) vs. invasive honeysuckles: snap the stem. Solid pith = native. Hollow pith = invasive. Also, native honeysuckle has paired tubular flowers; invasive species have smaller, more numerous flowers. Jewelweed (Impatiens capensis) vs. Himalayan balsam (Impatiens glandulifera): jewelweed is native, shorter (3–5 feet), with orange spotted flowers. Himalayan balsam is taller (6–10 feet) with pink-purple flowers and is invasive, especially along waterways. Virginia creeper (Parthenocissus quinquefolia) is a native vine sometimes confused with oriental bittersweet or other invasive vines. Virginia creeper has five leaflets arranged like a hand. It's a valuable native plant — leave it alone.

content.heading: What You Can Do
content.text: Individual action matters enormously with invasive species. Small infestations are far easier to control than established ones, so early detection and rapid response is the most effective strategy. For your own property: learn to identify the Big Five and remove them when you find them. Pull garlic mustard before it sets seed (ideally in April–May during flowering). Cut and treat bittersweet vines to save trees they're strangling. Replace burning bush and barberry with native alternatives — winterberry, spicebush, and viburnum provide the same ornamental value with ecological benefits. For volunteer removal days: most groups provide training, tools, and guidance on what to pull and how. Typical spring removal events focus on garlic mustard (timing is critical — must be done before seeds mature in late May). Summer and fall events often target woody species like barberry, buckthorn, and honeysuckle. Wear long sleeves, gloves, and long pants. Bring water and a willingness to get muddy. The work is physical but deeply satisfying — you can see the difference immediately. Report new infestations through platforms like iNaturalist, EDDMapS (Early Detection & Distribution Mapping System), or your state's invasive species reporting system. Your observations help track the spread of invaders and prioritize management efforts.

content.heading: The Bigger Picture
content.text: Invasive species are not a problem that can be solved once and forgotten. New invaders continue to arrive — spotted lanternfly is expanding into New England from the mid-Atlantic states, and warming winters are allowing southern invasive plants to establish farther north. The key is sustained management, not eradication. In most cases, the goal isn't to eliminate every invasive plant but to reduce their dominance enough that native species can compete. A forest with some barberry in the understory can still support native wildflowers, salamanders, and nesting birds. A forest where barberry has formed a continuous thicket cannot. Every plant you pull opens space for a native to reclaim. Every vine you cut saves a tree. Every garlic mustard you bag before it seeds prevents thousands of future plants. It's unglamorous, incremental work — and it's some of the most impactful conservation action available to ordinary people.

Your invasive species starter kit — five plants to learn first: (1) Garlic mustard — crush a leaf, smell garlic, pull it. (2) Japanese barberry — thorny, small oval leaves, red berries, tick haven. (3) Oriental bittersweet — vine with yellow-and-red berries at every node, strangling trees. (4) Multiflora rose — arching thorny thicket, fringed stipules at leaf base. (5) Bush honeysuckle — snap the stem; hollow = invasive. Learn these five and you'll be an effective volunteer on day one.

title: The Dark Side of the Forest: Parasitic Plants and Fungi
subtitle: The organisms that steal, manipulate, and devour their neighbors — and why they matter

content.text: Not everything in the forest makes its own food. Beneath the green canopy of photosynthesizing plants and the quiet decomposition work of fungi, a darker economy is running — one built on theft, manipulation, and exploitation. Parasitic plants steal water and nutrients from other plants. Parasitic fungi invade living trees, slowly consuming them from the inside. And some of the strangest organisms in New England blur the line between parasite and partner in ways that challenge our understanding of how ecosystems work. These aren't rare curiosities. They're everywhere, hiding in plain sight, and they play essential roles in forest health.

content.heading: What Is Parasitism in Nature?
content.text: A parasite is an organism that lives on or inside another organism (the host) and benefits at the host's expense. In the plant and fungal world, this takes many forms. Some parasites tap directly into another plant's vascular system to steal water and sugars. Some fungi penetrate living wood and slowly digest the tree from within. Others have evolved an even stranger strategy — they parasitize fungi rather than plants, tapping into the underground mycorrhizal networks that connect trees and fungi. The line between parasitism and other relationships is often blurry. A fungus that weakens a tree but also helps decompose deadwood is both a parasite and a recycler. A plant that steals from a fungal network but may also facilitate nutrient transfer is somewhere between thief and middleman. Nature rarely sorts itself into clean categories.

content.heading: Ghost Pipe: The Phantom of the Forest Floor
content.text: Indian pipe (Monotropa uniflora) — also called ghost pipe or corpse plant — is one of the most otherworldly organisms you'll encounter in New England. It's entirely white — stem, leaves, flower — because it has no chlorophyll and does no photosynthesis whatsoever. It looks like a small, waxy, translucent pipe rising from the leaf litter, often in clusters. When you first see one, you might not believe it's a plant at all. Ghost pipe is a mycoheterotroph — it parasitizes fungi. Specifically, it taps into the mycorrhizal fungi (usually Russula species) that are in mutualistic partnerships with nearby trees. The tree sends sugars to the fungus; the fungus shares some with the ghost pipe. In effect, ghost pipe is stealing from a partnership — a parasite of a mutualism. The tree is the ultimate source of energy, but the ghost pipe never touches the tree directly. It gets everything through the fungal middleman. Ghost pipe is an indicator of healthy, mature forest with intact mycorrhizal networks. If you find it, the underground fungal ecosystem is working. Look for it in deep shade on the forest floor from June through September, often near beech, oak, or pine.

content.alt: Ghost Pipe (Monotropa uniflora) — translucent white waxy stems rising from forest floor
content.caption: Ghost Pipe: completely lacking chlorophyll, this ethereal plant steals nutrients from fungi connected to tree roots

content.heading: Pinesap and the Mycoheterotroph Family
content.text: Ghost pipe isn't alone. It belongs to a small family of plants that have entirely abandoned photosynthesis. Pinesap (Monotropa hypopitys) is ghost pipe's close relative — similar in form but yellow, orange, or reddish rather than white, and bearing multiple nodding flowers per stem instead of one. It's less common than ghost pipe and favors coniferous or mixed forests. Coralroot orchids (Corallorhiza) are mycoheterotrophic orchids — they have no leaves and no green tissue. They produce a single stalk of small flowers rising from a branching, coral-like rhizome (hence the name). Spotted coralroot (C. maculata) and early coralroot (C. trifida) are the most common New England species. They parasitize fungi associated with tree roots, just like ghost pipe, but they've evolved this strategy independently from an entirely different branch of the plant family tree. Pinedrops (Pterospora andromedea) is a striking mycoheterotroph — a tall, reddish-brown stalk up to 3 feet tall, studded with urn-shaped flowers. It's rare in New England and a genuine find if you encounter one, usually in pine or spruce forests.

content.heading: Beechdrops and Squawroot: Tapping the Roots
content.text: While mycoheterotrophs steal from fungi, some parasitic plants go directly to the source and tap into tree roots themselves. Beechdrops (Epifagus virginiana) is obligately parasitic on American beech — it grows nowhere else. It's a slender, purplish-brown branching stem up to a foot tall, with small tubular flowers, found at the base of beech trees in autumn. It has no chlorophyll and no true leaves — just scales. Its roots form direct connections (haustoria) with beech roots, siphoning water and nutrients. If you know where beech trees grow, you can find beechdrops — look at the base of the trunk in September and October. Squawroot (Conopholis americana) — also called bear corn — parasitizes oak roots. It emerges as a thick, yellow-brown, cone-shaped structure that looks remarkably like a pine cone pushing up from the ground. It's actually a dense cluster of scale-like leaves and flowers. Bears dig them up and eat them (hence the name bear corn), and they're an important early spring food source for wildlife. Look for them at the base of oaks from April through June.

images.caption: Beechdrops

images.alt: American Cancer-root (Conopholis americana) — yellow-brown cone-like structure rising from soil
images.caption: Squawroot

content.caption: Root parasites: Beechdrops tap into beech tree roots, while Squawroot attaches to oak roots — both lack any green coloring

content.heading: Dodder: The Strangler Vine
content.text: Dodder (Cuscuta) is the most visually dramatic plant parasite in New England. It looks like someone threw tangled orange or yellow spaghetti over a shrub. Dodder is a true stem parasite — it wraps around host plants and inserts tiny penetrating organs called haustoria into the host's vascular tissue, stealing water, nutrients, and sugars directly. Here's what makes dodder remarkable: it starts life as a normal seedling rooted in soil. But it must find a host plant within days of germinating or it dies — it cannot sustain itself through photosynthesis. The seedling actually "sniffs" its way to a host, growing toward chemical signals released by nearby plants. Research has shown that dodder preferentially attacks certain species and can even "choose" healthier, more nutrient-rich hosts over weaker ones. Once attached, dodder abandons its root connection to the soil entirely. It becomes a fully aerial parasite, sometimes spreading from one host to the next, draping entire hedgerows in orange thread. New England has several dodder species, with Cuscuta gronovii (common dodder) being the most widespread, often found in wetlands and along stream banks parasitizing goldenrod, asters, and other herbaceous plants.

content.heading: Dwarf Mistletoe: New England's Only Mistletoe
content.text: Most people associate mistletoe with the South or with holiday decorations, but New England has its own native mistletoe — dwarf mistletoe (Arceuthobium pusillum). It's tiny, easily overlooked, and parasitizes spruce trees in bogs and northern forests. Unlike the leafy mistletoes of warmer regions, dwarf mistletoe is just a few centimeters of olive-green to brownish stem emerging from spruce branches. It causes dense, bushy deformations in spruce branches called witches' brooms — abnormal clusters of short, stunted twigs that can grow to several feet in diameter. These brooms are actually more ecologically interesting than they appear — they provide nesting sites for birds and shelter for small mammals. Dwarf mistletoe has an explosive seed dispersal mechanism: ripe berries build up hydrostatic pressure and shoot their sticky seeds at speeds up to 60 miles per hour, landing on nearby branches where they stick, germinate, and start new infections.

content.heading: Honey Mushroom: The World's Largest Organism
content.text: Armillaria — the honey mushroom — is both one of the most common and most remarkable fungi in New England. It's a parasite that attacks living trees, killing them slowly by decomposing the wood beneath the bark, and then continues feeding on the dead tree as a saprophyte. It's a dual lifestyle — killer, then recycler. Honey mushrooms spread through the soil via thick, black, shoestring-like structures called rhizomorphs that can extend for meters through the ground, seeking new tree roots to infect. A single Armillaria individual can be enormous — the famous specimen of Armillaria ostoyae in Oregon covers 2,385 acres and is estimated to be thousands of years old, making it the largest and possibly oldest organism on Earth. New England's Armillaria colonies are smaller but still impressive. Honey mushrooms appear in autumn as clusters of golden-brown mushrooms at the base of infected trees or on the ground nearby. Armillaria mellea — the classic honey mushroom — has another remarkable trait: bioluminescence. Its mycelium glows faintly in the dark, producing an eerie greenish light called foxfire. In colonial times, people used luminous pieces of Armillaria-infected wood to mark paths through the forest at night.

content.alt: Honey Mushroom (Armillaria mellea) — cluster of golden-brown mushrooms at base of tree
content.caption: Honey Mushrooms look innocent but their underground network can span thousands of acres, slowly killing trees

content.heading: Cordyceps: The Zombie Makers
content.text: The genus Ophiocordyceps includes some of the most terrifying parasites on the planet. These fungi infect living insects, consume them from the inside, manipulate their behavior, and then produce a fruiting body that erupts from the dead host's body. The tropical species that zombifies ants — forcing them to climb to a precise height, clamp their jaws on a leaf, and die in a position optimal for spore dispersal — is famous from nature documentaries. New England's Cordyceps and Ophiocordyceps species are less dramatically mind-controlling but equally fascinating. Cordyceps militaris is the most commonly encountered species — it produces bright orange, club-shaped fruiting bodies that emerge from buried moth or butterfly pupae in the soil. Finding one means digging carefully to reveal the mummified insect at its base. Ophiocordyceps species in our region parasitize various insects including beetles, ants, and wasps. The fruiting bodies are often small and cryptic — thin, dark stalks emerging from a dead insect on the underside of a log or buried in leaf litter. Finding them takes patience and a willingness to look closely at things most people walk past.

content.heading: Bracket Fungi: The Slow Devourers
content.text: Walk through any New England forest and you'll see bracket fungi — shelf-like growths protruding from tree trunks. Many are parasites that entered through a wound and are slowly consuming the heartwood. Chaga (Inonotus obliquus) is the most distinctive — a black, charcoal-like, irregularly shaped mass (called a conk or sclerotium) that protrudes from birch trees. It looks more like a burnt growth than a mushroom. Chaga has become famous as a health supplement (chaga tea), though the scientific evidence for its benefits in humans is limited. What's certain is that it's a slow-acting parasite that eventually kills its host birch, typically over 10 to 20 years. Artist's conk (Ganoderma applanatum) is a large, flat bracket fungus with a white pore surface on the underside that bruises brown when scratched — you can literally draw on it, hence the name. It persists for years, adding a new layer of pore tissue each growing season. Hemlock varnish shelf (Ganoderma tsugae) — the glossy, reddish-brown bracket you find on dead and dying hemlocks — is closely related to the reishi mushroom (G. lucidum) used in traditional Asian medicine. Tinder fungus (Fomes fomentarius) — the hoof-shaped bracket on birch and beech — has been used by humans for thousands of years. Ötzi the Iceman, the 5,300-year-old mummy found in the Alps, carried pieces of Fomes, likely for starting fires.
