content.heading: Amphibians: Wetland Voices and Vernal Pool Breeders
content.text: New England's wetlands come alive with sound in spring. Spring peepers (Pseudacris crucifer) — tiny tree frogs smaller than a quarter — produce the deafening chorus of high-pitched whistles that defines March and April evenings across the region. A single swamp might contain thousands, each male calling from emergent vegetation or shrub branches. Wood frogs (Lithobates sylvaticus) breed explosively early — sometimes while ice still covers part of the pool — with a quacking chorus that lasts only a few days. They depend on fishless vernal pools within forested swamps. Spotted salamanders (Ambystoma maculatum) migrate to the same vernal pools on the first warm, rainy nights of spring — a spectacle called the "Big Night" that wildlife enthusiasts eagerly anticipate. Red-spotted newts (Notophthalmus viridescens) have a complex life cycle: aquatic larvae, terrestrial juvenile "red efts" (the bright orange salamanders you find on forest trails), and aquatic adults in permanent wetlands. Every stage depends on healthy wetland habitat.

content.heading: Wetland Birds and Mammals
content.text: Great blue herons (Ardea herodias) are the sentinels of New England's swamps — standing motionless in shallow water, waiting to spear fish, frogs, or crayfish with their dagger-like bills. American bitterns (Botaurus lentiginosus) are the ghosts: cryptically streaked to match dead cattails, they freeze with their bill pointed skyward when threatened, becoming nearly invisible. Their deep, pumping "oonk-a-loonk" call is one of the eeriest sounds in a marsh. Wood ducks (Aix sponsa) — arguably North America's most beautiful duck — nest in tree cavities in forested swamps. Beavers (Castor canadensis) are the ecosystem engineers: their dams create wetlands where none existed, flooding forests and meadows to produce the ponds and marshes that support everything from herons to moose. A single beaver dam can transform an entire valley. Muskrats (Ondatra zibethicus) build their lodges in marshes and slow streams, and their feeding platforms — piles of cattail stems and roots — are conspicuous features of New England's marshes.

content.heading: Peat: A Time Capsule and Carbon Bank
content.text: The peat beneath a New England bog is a remarkable archive. Because decomposition is suppressed by acidity, cold, and waterlogging, peat preserves pollen grains, plant fragments, insect parts, and even chemical signatures of past atmospheric conditions. Scientists bore cores through peat deposits and read them like tree rings — the deepest layers date to the retreat of the glaciers, recording 12,000 years of vegetation history. Pollen analysis from New England bogs has reconstructed the entire post-glacial forest succession: tundra, then spruce-fir, then pine, then the hardwood forests we see today. Peat is also an enormous carbon store. Globally, peatlands contain twice as much carbon as all the world's forests combined, locked away in waterlogged, slowly decomposing plant matter. New England's bogs, while small compared to boreal peatlands, are locally significant carbon reservoirs. When bogs are drained or disturbed, the peat oxidizes and releases that stored carbon as CO2 — one reason why wetland conservation has become part of climate strategy.

content.heading: Threats and Conservation
content.text: New England has lost over half its original wetland acreage since European settlement — drained for agriculture, filled for development, or degraded by road construction and altered hydrology. Bogs are especially vulnerable because their chemistry depends on isolation from mineral-rich water; a road cut or drainage ditch that introduces groundwater can shift a bog toward fen conditions, eliminating the specialized bog species. Nutrient pollution from agricultural runoff and atmospheric nitrogen deposition favors aggressive, common species over the rare specialists that make bogs and fens unique. Invasive species — glossy buckthorn, purple loosestrife, common reed (Phragmites) — can overrun wetlands, displacing native plant communities. Climate change threatens bogs through warmer temperatures (accelerating peat decomposition), altered precipitation, and shifting species ranges. The good news: wetland protection is now strong under federal and state law (the Clean Water Act, state wetland protection acts), and many of New England's finest bogs and fens are protected in nature preserves, state parks, and conservation land.

content.heading: Where to Experience New England's Wetlands
content.text: Many of New England's best bogs have boardwalks for public access. Orono Bog Boardwalk in Maine offers a mile-long walk through a classic raised bog with pitcher plants, sundews, and leatherleaf. Eshqua Bog in Vermont (managed by The Nature Conservancy) is a calcareous fen famous for showy lady's slipper orchids. Hawley Bog in western Massachusetts is a National Natural Landmark — a quaking sphagnum bog with black spruce and tamarack. Pontook Reservoir bog in northern New Hampshire has classic boreal bog vegetation. In Connecticut, Cathedral Pines Bog Preserve has boardwalk access to an acidic peatland. For swamps, any state forest or Audubon sanctuary with red maple wetlands will give you the forested swamp experience, especially in April when vernal pools are active and wood frogs are calling. The key timing: visit bogs in June-July for pitcher plant flowers and orchids, and swamps in March-April for amphibian breeding.

Here's the quick field test to tell if you're in a bog, fen, or swamp. First: are there trees? If the wetland is forested, it's a swamp (or the forested margin of a bog). If it's open with low shrubs and mosses, it's a bog or fen. Second: squeeze the ground surface. If you can wring water out of sphagnum moss and the water is tea-colored and acidic-smelling, you're in a bog. If the ground is firm with sedges and grasses, and the water is clearer, you're in a fen. Third: look for carnivorous plants. Pitcher plants and sundews strongly indicate bog conditions — they've evolved to eat insects because the soil can't feed them. Sedge meadows with diverse wildflowers suggest fen. Fourth: the bounce test. Step onto a sphagnum mat in a true bog and you'll feel it bounce — you're standing on a floating mat of vegetation over water. This "quaking bog" sensation is unmistakable and unforgettable (and perfectly safe on well-established mats, though stay on boardwalks where provided).

title: Night Sounds: Identifying What You Hear After Dark
subtitle: A listener's guide to the frogs, insects, owls, and mammals that fill New England's nights with sound

content.text: Step outside on a New England evening from March through October and you're surrounded by sound — an orchestra of frogs, insects, owls, and mammals, each species producing a distinctive call that carries through the darkness. Most people hear these sounds constantly but can't name a single one beyond "crickets" (which may not even be crickets). Learning to identify night sounds is one of the most rewarding naturalist skills because it requires zero equipment, works in total darkness, and reveals an entirely hidden layer of biodiversity. A warm July evening in a New England suburb might have a dozen species calling simultaneously: tree crickets, katydids, green frogs, gray treefrogs, and a barred owl. Every sound has a source, a purpose, and a season. Once you start learning them, you'll never hear a summer night the same way again — the undifferentiated wall of sound separates into individual voices, each telling you exactly who's out there and what they're doing.

content.heading: Spring Peepers: The Sound of Spring
content.text: The first great sound of the New England year is the spring peeper chorus. Starting in mid-March (southern New England) to mid-April (northern), these tiny tree frogs — barely an inch long — produce a sound so loud that a full chorus can be heard a mile away. Each male peeper produces a single, clear, high-pitched "peep" about once per second, but when hundreds or thousands call together from a wetland, the individual peeps merge into a deafening, pulsing wall of sound — like sleigh bells played at concert volume. Spring peepers (Pseudacris crucifer) call from emergent vegetation, shrub branches, and leaf litter around shallow wetlands, vernal pools, and flooded ditches. The tiny "X" mark on their back gives them their species name (crucifer = cross-bearer). They call on warm, humid evenings, and a late cold snap will silence them overnight — then the first warm rain starts them up again. The peeper chorus is so associated with spring that for many New Englanders, hearing the first peepers is the true start of the season, more meaningful than any calendar date.

content.heading: Wood Frogs, Toads, and the Frog Calendar
content.text: New England's frogs call in a predictable sequence through spring and summer, and learning the order lets you read the calendar by ear. Wood frogs (Lithobates sylvaticus) are the earliest — their explosive, duck-like quacking from vernal pools can start in late February during thaws. They call for only a few days, breed, and go silent. American toads (Anaxyrus americanus) start their long, musical trills in April — a high, sustained, beautiful note lasting 10-30 seconds that resonates from garden edges, ditches, and shallow pools. Gray treefrogs (Dryophytes versicolor) begin in May with a loud, musical trill shorter and more staccato than the toad's — they call from trees and shrubs, and their call carries an astonishing distance for a two-inch frog. Green frogs (Lithobates clamitans) call from pond edges all summer with a sound like plucking a loose banjo string — a single, twangy "gung." Bullfrogs (Lithobates catesbeianus) produce the deep, resonant "jug-o-rum" bass note from larger ponds and lakes. Pickerel frogs (Lithobates palustris) have a low, steady snore. Each species has its season, its habitat, and its voice.

content.heading: Tree Crickets: The Thermometer of the Night
content.text: The continuous, rhythmic chirping that fills summer and early autumn nights across New England comes primarily from tree crickets — pale green, delicate insects that call from shrubs, trees, and tall vegetation. Snowy tree crickets (Oecanthus fultoni) produce the classic, steady, pulsing chirp that most people associate with "a summer night." Here's the remarkable thing: their chirp rate is directly tied to temperature. Count the number of chirps in 13 seconds and add 40, and you get the current temperature in Fahrenheit — a formula called Dolbear's Law, and it's surprisingly accurate. On cool nights (50s F), tree crickets chirp slowly and deliberately. On hot nights (80s+), the chirping accelerates into a rapid pulse. Other tree cricket species have slightly different songs: four-spotted tree cricket (Oecanthus quadripunctatus) has a faster, continuous trill, and black-horned tree cricket (Oecanthus nigricornis) produces a more stuttering pattern. Tree crickets call from late July through the first hard frost — their season ending is as much a marker of autumn's arrival as falling leaves.

content.heading: Field Crickets: The Bass Section
content.text: Field crickets produce the loud, rich, musical chirping you hear from ground level — under porches, along stone walls, in gardens, and in leaf litter. They're louder and lower-pitched than tree crickets, with a robust, cheerful quality. Fall field cricket (Gryllus pennsylvanicus) is the most common species in New England, calling from late summer through autumn. Spring field cricket (Gryllus veletis) has a nearly identical song but calls earlier in the year — the two species were only recognized as distinct in the 1950s because they look nearly identical but have different life cycles (spring crickets overwinter as late-instar nymphs, fall crickets as eggs). Male crickets chirp by rubbing a scraper on one wing against a file on the other — a process called stridulation. Only males sing, and they produce different calls for different purposes: a loud calling song to attract females from a distance, a softer courtship song when a female is nearby, and an aggressive rivalry chirp when another male encroaches.

content.heading: Katydids: The Treetop Chorus
content.text: True katydid (Pterophylla camellifolia) produces the loud, rasping "katy-did, katy-didn't" call from high in deciduous trees on summer nights — one of the most recognizable insect sounds in eastern North America. Despite being incredibly loud and common, katydids are almost never seen — their leaf-green wings provide perfect camouflage in the canopy. Angular-winged katydids (Microcentrum) produce sharp, loud "ticks" — individual clicks spaced a few seconds apart from shrubs and lower tree branches. Bush katydids (Scudderia) make rapid sequences of lisping buzzes from shrubs and meadow edges. Cone-headed katydids (Neoconocephalus) are the buzzsaw of the insect world — their continuous, intense, high-pitched buzzing can be almost painfully loud at close range and carries hundreds of yards. Meadow katydids (Conocephalus) produce soft, high-pitched, continuous buzzing from grasses and low vegetation — they're the background hum you might not even consciously notice until you learn to listen for it. Together, katydids create much of the dense, layered sound texture of a New England summer night.

content.heading: Barred Owl: Who Cooks for You?
content.text: The barred owl (Strix varia) is New England's most commonly heard owl — its classic call, transcribed as "who cooks for you, who cooks for you-all," echoes through mature forests year-round but especially during breeding season (February-March). The pattern is unmistakable: eight hooted syllables, with the last one trailing downward. But barred owls have a much larger repertoire than the textbook call. Mated pairs often engage in wild, chaotic duets — a cacophony of hoots, cackles, barks, and screams that can sound like demented monkeys. These duets carry far and are genuinely startling if you don't know what you're hearing. Barred owls call actively at dusk and after dark, and they respond to playback and imitation — cup your hands around your mouth and give a passable "who cooks for you" and you may get a real owl answering back. They're large, stocky, dark-eyed owls of mature forests with access to water, and they're increasing throughout New England as forests mature.

content.heading: Great Horned Owl and Eastern Screech Owl
content.text: The great horned owl (Bubo virginianus) has the deepest, most resonant hoot of any New England owl — a deep, booming "hoo-hoo-HOO-hoo-hoo" that carries enormous distances on still winter nights. They begin calling in December and January, the earliest nesting bird in the region, sometimes incubating eggs while snow covers their nest. Their call pattern is typically five hoots, with the third loudest and highest. Males and females duet, the female's voice slightly higher. Great horned owls are powerful predators that eat skunks, rabbits, and even other owls — they're the reason barred owls sometimes go quiet. Eastern screech owl (Megascops asio) is small (robin-sized) but produces haunting calls that carry well through suburban neighborhoods and forest edges. Its two main calls are a descending whinny (a ghostly, trembling whistle that drops in pitch) and a monotone trill on a single pitch. Both sound eerie and are commonly mistaken for "something weird" by people unfamiliar with them. Screech owls are common in suburbs with mature trees.

content.heading: Saw-whet Owl and Whip-poor-will
content.text: Northern saw-whet owl (Aegolius acadicus) is New England's smallest owl and produces one of the most monotonous sounds in nature: a steady, rhythmic "toot-toot-toot-toot" repeated at about two toots per second, continuing for minutes or even hours without pause. It sounds mechanical — like a truck backing up in the distance or a slow, rhythmic beeping. Saw-whet owls call primarily in late winter and spring (February-April) from dense coniferous or mixed forests. Their small size and nocturnal habits make them virtually invisible, but their call is distinctive once learned. Eastern whip-poor-will (Antrostomus vociferus) is the legendary voice of warm summer nights — a loud, endlessly repeated "whip-poor-WILL" that can go on for hundreds of repetitions without pause. Whip-poor-wills call from forest edges and openings at dusk and through moonlit nights. Sadly, they've declined dramatically in New England due to habitat loss and declining moth populations (their primary food). Hearing one today is increasingly special — report it if you do.

content.heading: Dusk Singers: Thrushes and Woodcock
content.text: The transition from day to night — the half hour around sunset — has its own signature sounds. Wood thrush (Hylocichla mustelina) sings a flute-like, ethereal song often described as the most beautiful bird song in North America. It's a series of musical phrases, each ending with a harmonic trill created by the bird singing two notes simultaneously with its syrinx. Wood thrushes sing most actively at dusk and dawn from the interior of mature deciduous forests. Hermit thrush (Catharus guttatus) has a similar ethereal quality but is more spiraling — ascending, flute-like notes that seem to dissolve into the evening air. Veery (Catharus fuscescens) produces a descending, spiraling "veer" that sounds like water going down a drain — an otherworldly, echoing cascade of notes. American woodcock (Scolopax minor) performs one of nature's strangest courtship displays at dusk in spring: the male gives a nasal "peent" from the ground, then launches into the sky on whistling wings, spiraling upward hundreds of feet before tumbling back down in a zig-zag descent with liquid, chirping song. Find a damp field or woodland opening at dusk in March-April and listen for the "peent."

content.heading: Mammal Sounds: The Startling Ones
content.text: Some of the most alarming sounds you'll hear at night come from mammals. Red fox (Vulpes vulpes) produces a blood-curdling scream — a single, sharp, high-pitched shriek that sounds like a woman screaming in the woods. It's a contact call between foxes, most common during winter mating season (January-February), and it terrifies people who don't know what it is. Eastern coyote (Canis latrans) produces elaborate group howling sessions — a mix of howls, yips, barks, and wails that makes a small pack sound like dozens. Coyote howling peaks in late winter (breeding) and late summer (pups practicing). The sound carries miles and is increasingly common even in suburban New England. Raccoons (Procyon lotor) produce a surprising range of sounds: chattering, purring, growling, and a high-pitched screeching during confrontations. Flying squirrels (which are nocturnal and far more common than most people realize) produce high-pitched, bird-like chirps that people often attribute to unknown birds.

content.heading: Moths and Bats: The Silent Majority
content.text: Not all night creatures make sounds humans can hear, but they're worth knowing about. Luna moths (Actias luna) — the spectacular, large, pale green moths with long tail streamers — are active on warm nights from May through July. Cecropia moths (Hyalophora cecropia), North America's largest native moth with wingspans reaching 6 inches, are equally nocturnal and equally silent. Polyphemus moths (Antheraea polyphemus) have enormous eyespots on their hindwings. Io moths (Automeris io) flash bright eyespots when disturbed. All of these giant silk moths are attracted to lights, so a porch light on a warm June night may bring stunning visitors. Bats are common nighttime presences — little brown bats (Myotis lucifugus) and big brown bats (Eptesicus fuscus) emerge at dusk to hunt insects, producing echolocation calls above human hearing range. You can detect them with a bat detector (or some phone apps) that converts their ultrasonic calls into audible clicks and buzzes. Bat populations have been devastated by white-nose syndrome, making every bat sighting worth noting on iNaturalist.

content.heading: The Seasonal Sound Calendar
content.text: Night sounds follow a reliable seasonal progression in New England. Late February-March: great horned owl hoots, woodcock "peenting," wood frog quacking from vernal pools. March-April: spring peeper chorus builds to full volume, saw-whet owl tooting, American toad trills begin. May: gray treefrog trills join in, whip-poor-will begins, wood thrush sings at dusk, first crickets. June-July: full insect chorus develops — tree crickets, field crickets, early katydids. Green frogs and bullfrogs calling from ponds. Giant silk moths at porch lights. Late July-September: peak insect chorus — katydids, cone-heads, and tree crickets at full volume. This is the densest sound period of the year. Frog calls winding down. September-October: insect chorus thins as frosts arrive. Tree crickets slow their chirp rate noticeably on cool nights. Barred owl calls increase as fall territory defense begins. November-February: quietest period. Great horned owl courtship hoots. Fox screams. Coyote howls carry far through leafless, frozen air.

content.heading: How to Learn Night Sounds
content.text: The best approach is to learn a few distinctive species first, then build from there. Start with the five sounds that almost everyone in New England can hear from home: spring peepers (March-April, the massed high-pitched chorus), American toad (April-May, the long sustained trill), barred owl (year-round, "who cooks for you"), field cricket (August-October, the classic cricket chirp), and true katydid (July-September, "katy-did katy-didn't" from treetops). Once you have those five locked in, add more by listening for unfamiliar sounds and trying to track them down. Go to known frog ponds at dusk in spring and match what you hear to recordings. Stand in a meadow on an August evening and try to separate the insect voices — the high continuous buzz (meadow katydids), the pulsing chirps (tree crickets), the deeper chirping (field crickets), the rasping calls (true katydids). The Macaulay Library at Cornell (free online) has recordings of every species, and apps like Merlin can identify bird calls in real time using your phone's microphone.

Try a "sound sit" — find a spot near a wetland or forest edge on a warm evening in May or June, sit still for 20 minutes, and just listen. For the first few minutes, you'll hear a wall of undifferentiated sound. But as your ears adjust, individual voices start to separate out, just like instruments in an orchestra. Focus on one sound at a time: isolate the highest-pitched voice (probably tree crickets or meadow katydids), then the lowest (bullfrogs or field crickets), then start picking apart the middle range. Use your phone to record a segment you can't identify, then compare it to recordings later. Over a few sessions, you'll build a mental library of sounds that lets you "read" a night soundscape instantly — knowing within seconds which frogs, insects, and owls are active, roughly how warm it is (from tree cricket chirp rate), and what time of the season you're in. It's like learning a new language where the landscape is the speaker.

title: Seaweed and Marine Algae of the New England Coast
subtitle: A beachcomber's guide to the greens, reds, and browns that carpet our rocky shores and fill our tidepools

content.text: Seaweed is the most overlooked group of organisms on the New England coast. People walk past it, step on it, complain about it on the beach, and rarely give it a second thought. But seaweed is the foundation of the coastal ecosystem — the underwater forest that feeds, shelters, and oxygenates everything from snails to lobsters. New England has over 300 species of marine algae, ranging from microscopic films on rocks to kelp forests swaying in offshore currents. They come in three major groups — green, brown, and red — each with distinctive biology and ecology. Unlike land plants, seaweeds have no roots, stems, or leaves. They absorb water and nutrients directly through their entire surface, anchor themselves with a holdfast (not a root), and photosynthesize with the same basic chemistry as land plants. Learning even a dozen common species transforms a walk on a rocky shore from "slippery nuisance" to "I know exactly what that is and why it grows there."

content.heading: Three Colors, Three Lineages
content.text: The green, brown, and red color groups aren't just descriptive — they represent three fundamentally different evolutionary lineages, each with different photosynthetic pigments that determine what wavelengths of light they can use. Green algae (Chlorophyta) have the same pigments as land plants — chlorophyll a and b — giving them their bright green color. They're the closest algal relatives of land plants, and they tend to dominate the upper intertidal and shallow pools where light is strongest. Brown algae (Phaeophyceae) have chlorophyll plus fucoxanthin, a golden-brown accessory pigment that lets them capture light wavelengths that penetrate deeper water. Browns dominate the mid-to-low intertidal and subtidal zones — they include the largest seaweeds (kelps). Red algae (Rhodophyta) have chlorophyll plus phycoerythrin and phycocyanin, pigments that capture the blue-green light that penetrates deepest in the ocean. Reds can grow in the dimmest conditions, living deeper than any other algae, though many common species also thrive in tidepools and on intertidal rocks.

content.heading: Sea Lettuce: The Bright Green Sheet
content.text: Sea lettuce (Ulva lactuca) is the most recognizable green alga on the New England coast — bright green, translucent, sheet-like fronds that look exactly like wilted lettuce leaves growing on rocks, in pools, and floating in sheltered bays. It's edible, nutritious (rich in iron and protein), and has been eaten by coastal peoples worldwide. You can eat it raw in salads, dry it into chips, or add it to soups. Ulva thrives in nutrient-rich waters, so heavy blooms in harbors and estuaries often indicate nitrogen or phosphorus pollution from runoff — it's a biological indicator of water quality, much as lichens indicate air quality. Gut weed (Ulva intestinalis) forms narrow, inflated, tube-like fronds that look like green intestines — it colonizes upper intertidal rocks and pools, especially in areas with fresh water seepage. Sea lettuce is one of the fastest-growing marine organisms, capable of doubling its biomass in a week under good conditions, which is why it's being studied as a potential sustainable food and biofuel crop.

content.heading: Dead Man's Fingers and Other Green Oddities
content.text: Dead man's fingers (Codium fragile) is an invasive green alga from the Pacific that has become common on New England shores since the mid-20th century. It forms dark green, spongy, finger-like branches up to a foot long, attached by a disc-shaped holdfast. Despite being a green alga, it appears dark green to almost black because of its dense, three-dimensional structure. It's often found washed up on beaches after storms, and its common name is well-earned — the rubbery, branching fingers are mildly unsettling. Codium causes economic problems by attaching to shellfish and smothering them or making them buoyant enough to wash away. Cladophora species form silky, bright green filaments that wave in tidepool currents like green hair. Bryopsis plumosa, the feather alga, forms delicate, fern-like plumes of bright green that are among the most beautiful structures in a tidepool when seen under a hand lens. Chaetomorpha species form coarse, dark green, unbranched filaments that look like tangled green wire — they're common in upper-shore pools and tolerant of wide salinity and temperature ranges.

content.heading: Rockweed: The Dominant Brown
content.text: Rockweed (Fucus species) and knotted wrack (Ascophyllum nodosum) are the dominant seaweeds of New England's mid-intertidal zone — the olive-brown, rubbery, branching algae that drape over every rock surface between the tidelines. At low tide, they collapse into a wet, slippery blanket; at high tide, their gas-filled bladders buoy them upright, creating an underwater canopy that shelters periwinkles, crabs, and dozens of other species. Rockweed is the foundation species of the rocky intertidal — without it, the entire community shifts. New England has several Fucus species: bladder wrack (F. vesiculosus) has paired air bladders along its fronds, spiral wrack (F. spiralis) has twisted, bladderless tips in the upper intertidal, and serrated wrack (F. serratus) has saw-toothed edges in the lower zone. Knotted wrack (Ascophyllum nodosum) has single, egg-shaped bladders spaced along long, strap-like fronds — it dominates sheltered shores and can live for decades, growing slowly. Rockweed harvesting is a commercial industry in Maine, where it's used for fertilizer, animal feed, and food products.

content.heading: Kelp Forests: The Underwater Giants
content.text: Kelp forests are the marine equivalent of terrestrial forests — towering, three-dimensional habitats that support entire ecosystems. Sugar kelp (Saccharina latissima) has a single, broad, ruffled blade that can grow several feet long from a short stipe (stem) and holdfast. It's the most common kelp in New England's subtidal zone and increasingly farmed commercially — it has a sweet, umami flavor and is used in restaurants and food products throughout the region. Winged kelp (Alaria esculenta) has a prominent midrib running down its blade and short, ruffled reproductive blades (sporophylls) at the base. Horsetail kelp (Laminaria digitata) has a broad blade split into finger-like divisions. These kelps grow on rocky substrate from the low intertidal into the subtidal, forming canopies that shelter juvenile fish, lobsters, sea urchins, and hundreds of invertebrate species. New England's kelp forests have been declining due to warming ocean temperatures — Gulf of Maine waters are warming faster than 99% of the global ocean, stressing cold-adapted kelp species.

content.heading: Irish Moss: Red Gold
content.text: Irish moss (Chondrus crispus) is arguably New England's most economically important seaweed. This dark red-purple, rubbery, fan-shaped alga forms dense turfs on low-intertidal and subtidal rocks throughout the region. It's harvested for carrageenan — a polysaccharide extracted from the cell walls that acts as a thickener, stabilizer, and gelling agent. Check the ingredients on your ice cream, chocolate milk, toothpaste, or salad dressing and you'll likely find carrageenan. The Irish moss industry in New England dates to the 1800s, and Scituate, Massachusetts, was once the capital of carrageenan production. Irish moss is also edible directly — it can be boiled into a thick, pudding-like dessert (blancmange) that was a traditional food in coastal Ireland and Maritime Canada during famines. In tidepools, Irish moss is easy to identify: its fronds are flat, repeatedly branching, and fan-shaped, with a tough, rubbery texture. Color varies from dark purple-red in shaded areas to yellow-green in sun-bleached upper pools.
